newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Boonstra says Philips tackling problems.
newsitem.headline: Boonstra says Philips tackling problems.

text.p: Cor Boonstra, the new chairman of Philips Electronics, said on Thursday that the electronics group was in a strong financial position and aimed to tackle its profit problems head on.
Philips earlier stunned the market with a slump in third quarter net from normal operations to 123 million guilders from 539 million -- off the scale of analysts' forecasts.

"I know we've had a bad quarter...we have decided that we are going to tackle our problems more aggressively," Boonstra told reporters at his first results news conference since taking over from Jan Timmer on October 1.

Philips said it planned to take a fourth quarter restructuring charge of one billion guilders, added to the 800 million guilder gross charge for a restructuring it announced at its Sound & Vision unit in July.
The latest charge will take in restructuring underperforming units elsewhere, across the range of Philips activities.

"I will also take head on what I call the bleeders in the company, that means we will turn around, sell or close businesses that are not performing to our standards or are not fitting into our portfolio. In the coming months we will communicate this to you step by step," Boonstra said.
Boonstra acknowledged that markets and investors were hungry for fresh clues on Philips' strategy after he replaced Timmer as chairman, but said addressing the restrucuturing was a primary focus.
"When the roof is leaking, fix it before you buy a new kitchen. I will come back to you on the subject of corporate strategy, we're looking at it, but first things first."

He took pains to point out that Philips was not in the same position as it was in the early 1990s when Timmer brought in the Centurion recovery progamme, hauling the firm back from the brink of disaster after big losses.
"The company six years ago was in a state of danger of bankruptcy. That is not the case today. We are in a financically much better position," Boonstra said.

He said the company was aiming for double-digit growth in 1997 income from operations and the firm had set a target for 24 percent return on net operating capital (RONA). In the first nine months of 1996 this was 8.4 percent.

"My job is to lead our manangement in unlocking the value of this company, we simply have to add shareholder value. Our shares are underperforming the average stock performance for the last 10 years. That's nothing to be proud of," he said. -- Keiron Henderson, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
